documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
CC: chest tightness.

HPI: For about six weeks she has had episodes of a tight feeling in the center of her chest that come on at
rest, mostly early in the morning before she gets up, sometimes waking her. Each lasts about 15 minutes and goes
away on its own. Not brought on by walking or stairs. No sweating, nausea, or shortness of breath with them. No
palpitations. Nothing today. Has not tried anything for them.

Meds: lithium carbonate 300 mg BID; amlodipine 5 mg daily; sumatriptan 100 mg PRN. NKDA.
Never smoker.

Exam: comfortable. Heart regular, no murmur, rub or gallop. Lungs clear. Chest wall not tender. No edema.

ECG in office: normal sinus rhythm, no ST changes.

A/P: Episodic rest chest discomfort, early morning, self-limited, normal resting ECG. Not typical of exertional
angina; reflux or musculoskeletal less likely given the timing and quality. Would like cardiology to see her
soon. Referral placed, front desk to get the first available.
Reviewed: call 911 for chest pain lasting more than 20 minutes, or with fainting or shortness of breath.

Just letting you know I saw cardiology Monday. I actually had one of the chest episodes right there in the

arteries of the heart, kind of like my fingers. I stay on the amlodipine and they gave me nitroglycerin to put
under my tongue if it happens. They said they'd send you a letter.

documents.title: RE: Saw the cardiologist

If the nitroglycerin doesn't relieve an episode, or one lasts longer than usual, call 911.

CARDIOLOGY CONSULTATION (received 12/11/2023)
Date of service: 10/23/2023
Referring: primary care

Reason for referral: chest pain at rest.

HPI: 45-year-old woman with a chronic vasospastic disorder followed by rheumatology who describes chest pain at
rest, usually in the early morning. She characterizes it as a constricting sensation of about 15 minutes that
goes away by itself. She also describes her fingers turning white and then blue in the cold or when she is
emotionally stressed. She has migraine and uses sumatriptan as needed.

Medications: lithium carbonate 300 mg BID; amlodipine 5 mg daily; magnesium oxide 400 mg at bedtime.
Allergies: NKDA.
Social: nonsmoker.

Exam: BP 130/85, HR 72, RR 16. Cardiac exam unremarkable without murmurs, rubs or gallops. No peripheral
edema.

During her early-morning appointment she developed a typical episode in clinic. A 12-lead ECG obtained during
the pain showed transient ST-segment elevation, which resolved with the symptom.

Labs: troponin I within normal limits. Triglycerides 100 mg/dL.

Assessment: Vasospastic (variant) angina.

Plan:
- Continue amlodipine 5 mg daily.
- Nitroglycerin 0.4 mg SL as needed for episodes, up to 3 doses 5 minutes apart; call 911 if unrelieved.
- Follow up in about 6 months.

Cardiology

documents.title: Endocrinology consultation
documents.author: endocrinology
documents.body:
ENDOCRINOLOGY — NEW CONSULTATION AND RESULTS
Date of visit: 10/13/2025; results discussed by phone 10/17/2025
Referred by: primary care (urgent)

HPI: Ms. Brooks is a 47-year-old woman with bipolar disorder on long-term lithium and a prior episode of
lithium-related hypothyroidism, who comes with ongoing thirst. She drinks roughly 4 to 5 liters of water daily
and is often up at night to void. Sleep is poor. She has lost about 5 pounds while eating normally and feels
heat intolerant.

PMH: bipolar disorder; migraine; Raynaud phenomenon; vasospastic angina; prior drug-induced hypothyroidism.
PSH: tonsillectomy in childhood.
Medications (per list we were sent / patient): lithium carbonate 300 mg BID; sumatriptan 100 mg PRN (max
200 mg/day); amlodipine 5 mg daily; magnesium oxide 400 mg at bedtime.
Allergies: NKDA.
FHx: mother bipolar disorder; sister migraine; maternal grandmother hypothyroidism.
SHx: administrative assistant; never smoker; no alcohol.

Exam: vital signs within normal limits; weight 62.6 kg, height 165 cm, BMI 23. Fine tremor of the hands. Mild
lid lag. Thyroid neither enlarged nor tender.

Data: referring labs 10/06: TSH 0.06, free T4 2.4, sodium 145, creatinine 1.0, lithium 0.9.
Ours 10/13: TSH receptor antibody negative. TPO antibody 12 IU/mL. Serum osmolality 296, urine osmolality
145 mOsm/kg.
Thyroid ultrasound 10/16: normal size, no nodules, vascularity not increased.

Assessment:
1. Lithium-induced painless thyroiditis, thyrotoxic phase. Antibody negative, normal-sized gland without
   increased flow; not Graves.
2. Lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus: polyuria with dilute urine and high-normal serum sodium and
   osmolality.

Plan:
- Thyroiditis: expected to settle over weeks to months. We are deliberately not using a beta blocker given her
  vasospastic angina and Raynaud. Repeat TSH and free T4 in about 6 weeks.
- NDI: amiloride 5 mg daily started 10/17. Discussed with her psychiatrist, who prefers to continue lithium
  given years of stability; we agree. Please check BMP and lithium level one week after starting.
- Free access to water; she should not restrict fluids, and should seek care if unable to drink.
- Return 6 weeks.

Endocrinology

OUTPATIENT PSYCHIATRY — LETTER TO PRIMARY CARE
Date of visit: 11/03/2025

Dear colleague,

Thank you for the recent labs and for the endocrinology correspondence. Ms. Brooks remains euthymic. We
discussed the new diagnoses of lithium-related thyroiditis and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus at length,
including the option of moving to another mood stabilizer. Given her many years of stability on lithium she
prefers to continue, and I agree, with amiloride per endocrinology.

Plan: lithium carbonate 300 mg twice daily unchanged. Please continue lithium level and renal panel at least
every 6 months (more often while amiloride is new is reasonable). Next visit with us in 3 months.

Outpatient psychiatry

symptoms. Current medications per our list: lithium carbonate 300 mg BID, amlodipine 5 mg daily, amiloride
5 mg daily, sumatriptan PRN, magnesium oxide 400 mg qhs.

Endocrinology
